# The Cost of Intelligence, Episode 22: Claude Code’s Code Mode, Tested


### One test cut input tokens by a third, but the bill fell 17%. Plus World View Wednesday, the chip-stock seesaw, Anthropic below its IPO price, and Amazon’s mechanic.


[Strong Compute](https://substack.com/@strongcompute)


Nov 25, 2026


*Listen to this episode on [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/5hjBvv77o9WLsRWxI0qWi9) or watch it on [YouTube](https://youtu.be/wZQxsJGBTNg) .*


Welcome back to


**The Cost of Intelligence** , our comedy news show about the money behind AI. Each episode, Ben Sand reads the industry’s invoice and asks one question: are you getting more intelligence per dollar?


This week:


**World View Wednesday** steps back to the whole planet’s AI bill.


**The chip stocks** give back a big piece of Monday’s rally.


**Anthropic’s stock** trades below its IPO price for the first time.


**Amazon** buys a chip-tuning shop. Plus three cuts from the Department of Token Efficiency, starting with


**Claude Code’s new Code Mode** . Here’s the written version, with every source linked.


---


## World View Wednesday


Once a week, we step back and look at the whole planet’s AI bill. The numbers move slow. The bills still grow.


**Tokens a day.** tokensperday.com puts the world at about


**480 trillion tokens a day** as of Tuesday, up from about 472 trillion last Wednesday. That’s the site’s own estimate: it starts from a July count and projects it forward (


[tokensperday.com](https://tokensperday.com/) ). Spread across 8.2 billion people, that’s about


**58,000 tokens a day** each (our arithmetic). Most of us didn’t use ours. Somebody in engineering used yours.


**Two slices.** Alphabet said in October that its model APIs handle “nearly 32 billion tokens per minute” (


[Alphabet’s Q3 remarks](https://blog.google/company-news/inside-google/message-ceo/alphabet-earnings-q3-2026/) ). That’s about


**46 trillion a day** (our conversion). On OpenRouter, the top ten models ran about


**150 trillion tokens** in the week to November 23 (our sum of the ten rows), about


**21 trillion a day** : less than half of Google’s API traffic. A new Tencent model, Hy4 flash, came in at


**number two** (


[OpenRouter rankings](https://openrouter.ai/rankings) ).


**The chips.** Our sum of Epoch AI’s chip-sales data comes to about


**39 million H100s’ worth** of AI chips, nearly six times the 6.7 million at the end of 2024 (


[Epoch AI](https://epoch.ai/data/ai-chip-sales) ). On our last World View the count was 34 million: same dataset, newer vintage, as Epoch caught up on Nvidia’s results.


**The power.** The data centers running them draw


**more than 30 gigawatts** , our estimate from Epoch’s tracker. That’s close to New York State’s summer peak of 31.1 GW (


[EIA](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=68305) ). AI data centers used about


**half a percent** of the world’s electricity last year, and counting just that electricity, about


**a tenth of a percent** of all the energy the world used (


[Our World in Data, on IEA estimates](https://ourworldindata.org/how-much-energy-do-data-centers-and-artificial-intelligence-use) ). Last week the International Energy Agency projected that all data centers’ electricity use could


**double by 2030** , in its World Energy Outlook (


[Euronews on the IEA](https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/19/data-centre-energy-consumption-could-double-by-2030-straining-grids-iea-warns) ).


**The spending.** Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta are on track for


**more than $700 billion** of capital spending this year, by their own guidance plus analysts’ math (Microsoft reports on a fiscal year). Last year it was over $400 billion.


**The work.** All this to drive a future filled with


**Seesawing Intelligence** : the kind that goes up and down with the chip index. On our bet, it’s now doing about


**12%** of the hours all of us work (our estimate). American workers say generative AI saves them about


**2%** of their work hours, in the Real-Time Population Survey (


[St. Louis Fed, FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/RPSGENAITSALL) ). Mostly the meetings. You’re welcome.


---


## The seesaw: chip stocks


On Monday, the Philadelphia chip index jumped


**14%** after Nvidia’s board brought Jensen Huang back. On Tuesday it fell about


**8%** : in points, that wiped out more than half of Monday’s gain. Nvidia fell about


**6%** , and memory and neocloud stocks fell harder: CoreWeave lost about


**12%** . The Nasdaq slipped less than


**2%** (−1.5%), so the chips took this one on their own (


[Yahoo Finance, SOX](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/%5ESOX/history/) ;


[CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/24/nvidia-stock-jensen-huang-return.html) ).


Meanwhile, CNBC reports Jensen Huang will testify to the Senate Banking Committee on


**December 3** (


[CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/24/jensen-huang-nvidia-congress-gtc.html) ).


*Per-dollar verdict: the volatility is free. The tokens are not.*


---


## The IPO hangover


Anthropic’s stock dipped below its


**$83** IPO price on Tuesday, for the first time. It fell as low as


**$75.61** , then recovered to close at about


**$82** , still under the IPO price (


[Anthropic’s IPO pricing](https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropic-prices-initial-public-offering) ;


[price history](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/ant/history/) ;


[CNBC](https://cnbc.com/2026/11/24/anthropic-stock-ipo-price.html) ).


At the IPO, all seven co-founders sold shares at the IPO price: 3,378,378 shares each, about


**$280 million** apiece at $83 (


[TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/10/all-7-anthropic-founders-will-each-cash-out-about-250m-in-ipo/) , our math at the final price). Same day, same price. They carpooled to the exit.


---


## Amazon buys the mechanic


Amazon is buying Decart’s chip-tuning software for


**$7.5 billion** , Bloomberg reports; Amazon hasn’t confirmed the price (


[TechCrunch, citing Bloomberg](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/23/amazon-snaps-up-decarts-ai-optimization-tech-for-7-5b-as-it-prepares-to-sell-trainium-chips/) ). Decart’s software tunes AI models to run faster on Nvidia’s chips, Google’s TPUs and Amazon’s own Trainium, and Amazon plans to sell Trainium to outside customers.


If that price holds, it’s one of Amazon’s biggest deals ever. Only Whole Foods ($13.7B), Globalstar ($11.57B, still pending,


[Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/sectors/technology/articles/amazon-signs-11-57-billion-120533254.html) ) and MGM ($8.45B) cost more. Groceries, satellites, movies, and now a pit crew.


*Per-dollar verdict: Amazon bought the mechanic. Watch whose car gets fixed first.*


**Bonus: HPE.** HPE’s sales hit


**$14.5 billion** last quarter, up


**50%** from a year ago, and it took


**$4.5 billion** in orders for AI systems, more than double a year ago (


[HPE’s Q4 call](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/hpe/transcripts/742928-q4-2026/) ). Wall Street disagreed: HPE’s stock fell about


**16%** on Tuesday (


[price history](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/hpe/history/) ).


*Per-dollar verdict: their revenue is your line item.*


---


## The Department of Token Efficiency


Chainsaw sharpened. Invoices on the table.


**Cut one: Code Mode, new in Anthropic’s Claude Code.** Code Mode swaps a long list of tools for one code tool: the model writes a small script instead of shuttling every result back through its memory. Creator


**Nate Herk** tested it on four real business tasks. His input tokens per message fell by about


**a third** (about 60,000 to 38,000). With caching counted, his bill fell about


**17%** (


[Nate Herk](https://nate-herk.com/claude-code-mode-token-savings) ). A blog called


**tabishapps** ran its own test on a local model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) with no caching: the model read just


**9%** as many tokens, 12,788 instead of 140,809 (


[tabishapps](https://tabishapps.com/blog/code-mode-tool-calls-test/) ). Same idea, two very different tests. And if your tokens were already cached, you save less.


**The fine print:** Code Mode is experimental. Herk’s jobs were small, and it ran slower in three of his five comparisons.


**Cut two: a router at Traide.** Traide, a startup, built a model router that sends each helper job to the smallest model allowed to do it. The big model used to do


**65%** of the helper jobs; now it’s


**14%** . Traide says the helper work now costs


**45% less** . Then it did the honest math: that saving is about


**3%** of its whole AI bill. Helper jobs are just


**4%** of its bill; the lead model gets the other


**96%** , mostly re-reading what it already knows (


[Traide](https://thetraide.com/blog/right-sizing-ai-model-routing) ). They put the interns on cheaper models. Then they found out the boss spends all day re-reading his own emails.


**The fine print:** Traide reported this about itself, and it priced the savings as if the big model had done the work.


**Cut three: Axiometa and Condense.** Axiometa builds AI for hardware design. Its median agent turn used to cost


**45 cents** ; with a tool called Condense, it’s down to


**16 cents** , almost two-thirds less. Condense sits between the app and the model; it says it compresses what the agent sends with every request and manages the caching. The cache hit rate jumped from


**70% to 96%** , and some of the savings came from catching the agent calling the model twice (


[Condense](https://condense.chat/blog/axiometa/) ). Even the robots double-book.


**The fine print:** this is Condense’s own customer story. Condense says its tool cut costs about


**30%** ; agent fixes did the rest.


The Department of Token Efficiency. Fewer tools, smaller helpers, and stop paying twice.
